- Model consistently overestimates early in the forecast horizon, especially in the first 5–10 days, then gradually underestimates later days.
- Forecasts tend to be too high relative to true values during sharp downward price movements (e.g., after spikes), suggesting failure to capture sudden sell-off momentum.
- Model exhibits mean reversion bias: forecasts drift upward over time, but true values often dip below forecast mid-point, indicating model overconfident upward trend.
- Model fails to adjust for recent price drops — when true values drop sharply (e.g., from 65+ to 55+), forecasts remain stubbornly high.
- Forecasts often overshoot the true value by 2–5% in the first 3–5 days, then converge slowly — suggesting lag in recalibration after market shocks.
- Model underestimates the magnitude of price rebounds after sharp declines — e.g., after 55–60, forecasts rarely reach 60+ until later, while true values often recover faster.
- Forecasts show diminishing sensitivity to recent history — e.g., when history includes a 10–15% drop, model doesn’t adjust forecast downward enough.
- Model tends to ignore short-term volatility — e.g., when true values spike up or down sharply, forecasts remain flat or slowly adjust.
- Forecasts often lag behind true values by 1–3 days, especially during volatile periods — suggesting delayed reaction to new information.
- Model overestimates the “bottom” of a price drop — e.g., when true value reaches 50–55, forecast still holds 60–65, indicating failure to recognize support levels.
